children.value: The rods would add a fourth value, but they hardly contribute to color: in daylight they are saturated, and at night the cones are silent. Color vision in daylight therefore rests on three numbers.

This reduction is only an approximation. A spectrum is a continuous function with infinitely many values, and the three integrals keep only three of them. Much information is lost, and many different spectra produce the same three responses. Such spectra look identical to us. They are called
, and we compute an example in the subsection on CIE XYZ below.

Metamerism is also what makes color displays possible. Because only three numbers matter, three primary lights suffice to reproduce most colors: a display mixes red, green, and blue light so that the mixture excites the three cone types in the same proportions as the original spectrum. The primaries do not need to match the peaks of the cones; they only need to excite the three cone types differently enough. The family of RGB systems is designed for human vision in this sense. It may not work for animals with different cone sensitivities: a bird with a cone type for ultraviolet light sees patterns on a flower that no RGB display reproduces.
Besides RGB, many other color systems exist. The most common ones are:
(XYZ, xyY, Lab), defined by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) to link the physical signal to the perception of a typical human observer.
, the prevailing systems in computing since HP and Microsoft introduced sRGB in 1996.
, which convert the Cartesian RGB coordinates into cylindrical coordinates for hue and saturation, with lightness or value as the third component.

, which separate a brightness signal from two color-difference signals. The PAL television standard used YUV, the NTSC standard the related YIQ, and image and video compression such as JPEG and MPEG uses YCbCr. We do not discuss them further.
, the system of printing. It subtracts color from a white sheet: the inks absorb light, and a blend of cyan, magenta, yellow, and black inks produces the intended color. We do not discuss it further.
Human vision uses three types of cones, so three components are needed to represent the full range of colors. A common way to split a color into three components is the following:
is the visual perception of emitted or reflected light. It depends on the luminance of an object but is not proportional to it; the observer interprets it subjectively.

is the objective description of a color without its luminance. It has two independent components, hue and saturation. A chromaticity diagram shows the full range of visible chromaticities, the gamut of human vision. The subset that a device or a color space can reproduce is its

describes how closely a color matches a pure spectral color such as red, green, or blue. In the chromaticity diagram, we draw a line from the white point through the color until it hits the curved boundary. The wavelength at this point is the
of the color. Hue is often given as an angle around the white point.

describes how concentrated the light is around a single wavelength. A pure spectral color has saturation 1; white has saturation 0. In the chromaticity diagram, saturation is the distance from the white point relative to the maximum possible distance in that direction. Color science distinguishes saturation from the related terms
, which measure the strength of a color relative to the brightness of a white or in absolute terms. Informally, the three words are often used interchangeably.

The diagram is not perceptually uniform. Green lies much farther from the white point than red or blue: the distance from D65 to the spectral locus is 0.56 at 520 nm, but only 0.38 at 620 nm and 0.34 at 460 nm. This large green region is an artifact of the diagram, not a sign that humans see more shades of green. We return to this problem with CIE Lab.

The CIE defined its color spaces to represent how people see color, and the mathematics behind them is the basis of color management. In 1931, the CIE introduced the XYZ color space to model human color perception. The experiments behind it showed that people see green as brighter than red or blue when all have the same physical power; the sensitivity of the eye to brightness peaks at 555 nm. At night, the rods take over from the cones. Vision becomes nearly monochrome and much more sensitive to dim light. The rod pigment absorbs best near 498 nm, and measured through the lens of the eye, night vision is most sensitive near 507 nm.
To compute X, Y, and Z from spectral data, the CIE defined a

from color matching experiments. It represents the average color response of a typical person within a 2 degree field in the fovea, the central region of the retina where most cones are concentrated. Lamps with three narrow emission bands exploit this effect.

CIE XYZ is widely used in colorimetry, color management, and image processing. It is the basis of the color spaces CIE Lab, CIE Luv, and CIE LCh, which serve for color communication and calibration in printing, photography, and display technology.

The CIE xyY space covers all colors that the standard observer sees, and it is a widely used color specification. It describes color as the standard observer sees it, not the inherent color of an object: the perceived color of an object changes with the lighting and with the color temperature of the light source. In low light, the human eye cannot see color at all and is limited to shades of gray. By including all colors of the standard observer, xyY links human perception to digital color systems and supports consistent color reproduction across devices.

RGB is the main color model in computing. HP and Microsoft proposed sRGB in 1996 as an additive standard color space for monitors, printers, and the Internet. It became the standard IEC 61966-2-1:1999, and software assumes it whenever an image does not specify its color space.

sRGB takes its primaries from the HDTV standard ITU-R BT.709, also called Rec. 709. They define its color gamut, the range of colors it can produce. The primaries became widely used because they matched the CRT monitors of the time. The chromaticities of the primaries and the white point are:

The nonlinear encoding is not a defect. The middle code value 128 corresponds to only 21.6 percent of the light, yet it looks like a medium gray, with a CIE Lab lightness of 53.6 out of 100. The encoding spends more code values on dark tones, where the eye distinguishes small differences, and fewer on bright tones. This is why 8 bits per channel suffice for most images.

Apart from sRGB and linear RGB, many other RGB spaces exist. We can create an RGB space simply by choosing three primaries and a white point. Alternative spaces extend the limited gamut of sRGB to a wider range of colors. To move an image from one RGB space to another, we decode it to linear values, convert to XYZ with the matrix of the source space, and convert back with the inverse matrix of the target space.

The CIE xyY space covers the entire range of visible colors, but it is not perceptually uniform: two pairs of colors with the same distance can look very different depending on where they lie in the space. The CIE Lab color space, defined in 1976 and also written CIELAB or L*a*b*, was created to provide a more perceptually uniform scale. It covers all visible colors, so its gamut exceeds that of RGB spaces, and it is device independent. It is therefore commonly used to map colors between different systems.

children.value: , a formula from 1976 also called CIE76. The four boxes of

, (155, 200, 100), (255, 200, 100), (255, 100, 100), and (255, 0, 100), differ by 100 units in one sRGB channel between neighbors. In Lab, the three steps measure 42.7, 59.8, and 27.7. Equal steps in sRGB are thus far from equal steps in perception, and Lab makes the difference visible in the numbers.

Lab is only approximately uniform. It is known to be least uniform for blue hues, and later formulas such as CIEDE2000 correct the Euclidean distance with weights for lightness, chroma, and hue. For color histograms and similar features, the plain Euclidean distance in Lab is usually good enough and much cheaper.
